name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,515

clue.text: Need to forbid hugging before Dutch right winger gets covered in bruises

blocks.note: to forbid is to ban; it is split to hold the next piece
a need is a lack of something
D is the standard abbreviation for Dutch
a blue is a Conservative, the party of the political right in Britain, whose colour is blue

explanation.surface: A Dutch right-wing politician is banned from somewhere and ends up beaten.
explanation.walkthrough: BLUE for a Tory is British political shorthand: Conservative rosettes and campaign colours are blue. B(LACK)AN + D + BLUE.
explanation.definitionFit: BLACK-AND-BLUE is the idiom for skin heavily marked with dark bruising after a beating.

clue.text: Country hotels changing Ohio

blocks.note: anagram fodder, taken as printed
O is a dictionary abbreviation for the US state of Ohio

explanation.surface: An American hotel chain is changing things across its Ohio branches.
explanation.walkthrough: Ohio is more usually OH; the single letter O is the older abbreviation that Chambers still lists, and it supplies the one letter the hotels lack.
explanation.definitionFit: LESOTHO is a small kingdom in southern Africa, entirely surrounded by South Africa.

clue.text: Most inferior copy discovered in box

blocks.note: a chest is a large box
to ape is to copy or imitate

explanation.surface: A worthless forgery turns up inside a box somebody has opened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copy' looks like a noun, the forgery of the surface, but it is the verb to imitate. 'Discovered' is not unmasked here; it means found inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheap can mean shoddy or of poor quality, so the superlative describes the worst-made of several things.

clue.text: Prove to be true when party's leader falls

blocks.note: a rave is a large dance party

explanation.surface: Evidence is confirmed on the day a political party's leader is toppled.
explanation.walkthrough: RAVE with its R dropped from the top of the column to the foot gives AVER. The political 'party' is a disguise for a dance party.
explanation.definitionFit: To aver is, in legal usage, to verify or allege formally as a fact; everyday usage is to assert firmly.

clue.text: Screen favourite cut over playing lad almost nude

indicators.note: 'almost' says the word for bare falls one letter short of complete

blocks.note: to dock is to cut short, as with a tail or wages
anagram fodder, taken as printed
NUDE without its final letter

explanation.surface: A film star's nude scene with a young man gets cut from the picture.
explanation.walkthrough: DO(NALDDU)CK. The joke is that the cartoon duck famously wears a sailor shirt and no trousers, so he really is almost nude.
explanation.definitionFit: The Disney cartoon character has been a much-loved film and television star since the 1930s.

clue.text: General keeping odd characters in view from riverside embankment

indicators.note: only the first and third characters of the following word, those in odd positions, are used

blocks.note: Robert E Lee, the Confederate commander, is the crossword's stock general
letters one and three of the word

explanation.surface: A general surveys the scene from a raised bank beside a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From' is a link: the answer comes from the wordplay before it. Lee is the stock crossword general.
explanation.definitionFit: A levee is a raised bank built along a river to stop it flooding, especially on the Mississippi.

clue.text: Aim to gamble in contest's final stage

blocks.note: an end is an aim or goal, as in 'to that end'
to game is an old verb meaning to gamble

explanation.surface: A competitor bets everything as a contest reaches its climax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To gamble' has to be read as a verb, and GAME in that sense survives in words like gaming and gamester.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess and other strategy contests the endgame is the last phase, when few pieces remain.

clue.text: Give details of spiritual care abroad

indicators.note: 'abroad' means scattered widely, so the two words are dispersed and reassembled

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

explanation.surface: A missionary describes pastoral work done overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abroad' reads as overseas in the surface, but in crosswords it also means all over the place, which is why it can signal an anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: To particularise is to treat something item by item, spelling out specifics one by one.

clue.text: Formerly working out with niece Pam after injury

indicators.note: the words have suffered injury, so their letters are damaged and rearranged

blocks.note: a machine that is on is working
anagram fodder, taken as printed
more anagram fodder, taken as printed

explanation.surface: A woman who used to exercise with her niece Pam gave it up after getting hurt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Working out' looks like one phrase about exercise, but it splits: 'working' is ON and 'out' joins the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The fairy-tale opening phrase simply means at some point in the past, a synonym of formerly.

clue.text: Gold head of Nabokov removed from novelist's grave

indicators.note: the head of a name is its opening letter, so just one letter of the Russian writer is meant

blocks.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
Laurence Sterne wrote Tristram Shandy
the letter taken away

explanation.surface: Gold is buried at a novelist's grave after one writer's name is removed.
explanation.walkthrough: With two novelists named, Nabokov only lends a letter; the novelist wanted is Laurence Sterne, author of Tristram Shandy. The 's is short for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe a serious, stern, unsmiling manner or appearance, so they are close synonyms.

clue.text: Article about Cameron withdrawn by New Statesman

indicators.note: to withdraw is to draw back, so the combined letters run backwards

blocks.note: an is the indefinite article
David Cameron, UK prime minister 2010 to 2016, was widely called Dave
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A magazine piece on David Cameron is pulled by the New Statesman, a British political weekly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New Statesman' must be split: New is N and Statesman is the definition, someone from a US state. A(DAVE)N reversed, then N.
explanation.definitionFit: A person from Nevada is literally a man of a state, a witty cryptic reading of statesman.

clue.text: Reckon on endless sheep appearing after a short time

indicators.note: 'endless' strips the final letter from the word before it

blocks.note: t is the standard abbreviation for time
ON minus its last letter
a tup is a ram, a word used in northern England and Scotland

explanation.surface: A farmer counts on a flock of sheep appearing after a little while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' looks as if it belongs with sheep, but it trims 'on'; the sheep is whole. TUP for a ram is a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: To reckon can mean to calculate, and to tot up is to add figures together into a sum.

clue.text: Set against foreign volunteers returning to Spain

blocks.note: alien means foreign
the TA, Territorial Army, was Britain's volunteer reserve force
E is the international vehicle code for Spain (España)

explanation.surface: International volunteers who fought in the Spanish Civil War head back to Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: TA for volunteers is a British convention: the Territorial Army was the part-time reserve.
explanation.definitionFit: To alienate someone is to make them hostile or estranged, turning them against a person or cause.

clue.text: As a consequence putting on nothing for women? Only occasionally

indicators.note: in a down entry, one piece put on another sits above it

blocks.note: no, as in 'no thing'
W is the standard abbreviation for women
'and then' introduces what follows as a result

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether women wear nothing as a result, and hears it happens seldom.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'putting on' means placing above, so the pieces for 'nothing for women' come first. The question mark flags the whimsical wording.
explanation.definitionFit: Now and then is an idiom for at irregular intervals, which means sometimes but seldom.

clue.text: Soap once made with religious symbol on Greek island they say

blocks.note: the cross is the Christian symbol
Rhodes is a large island in the Dodecanese

explanation.surface: Olive-oil soap once made on a Greek island and stamped with a cross.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soap' is a TV serial, not something to wash with; the setter exploits that by adding 'made'.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossroads was a long-running British television soap opera set in a Midlands motel, broadcast from 1964 to 1988.

clue.text: Observe with a sly look back

blocks.note: a peek is a quick furtive glance

explanation.surface: Someone watches, glancing slyly over their shoulder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Observe' seems to be about looking, fitting the surface, but it means to comply with, as in observing a rule or keeping a custom.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep a law, promise or festival is to observe it, honouring or following it faithfully.

clue.text: Study reportedly covering only Thailand proved to be incorrect

indicators.note: the sounded word is covering the others, wrapped around them

blocks.note: to read a subject is to study it, and said aloud it matches the waterside plant
but means only, as in 'but a child'
T is the international vehicle code for Thailand

explanation.surface: A research paper whose data covered only Thailand turns out to be wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: The homophone uses the present tense of the study word, which sounds like the marsh plant. Reading a subject is British university usage for studying it.
explanation.definitionFit: To rebut a claim is to refute it, showing by argument or evidence that it is false.

clue.text: Severely criticise after section's deleted near the end

blocks.note: to slate is to criticise harshly, British informal usage
s is an abbreviation for section, the letter removed

explanation.surface: A reviewer savages a piece once a section of it has been cut.
explanation.walkthrough: SLATE is British informal for criticising harshly, often used of reviews; losing the S leaves LATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Late describes a point toward the close of a period, as in late afternoon or late in the game.

clue.text: Paddy's social worker received by the president? Not quite

indicators.note: whatever is received by someone is taken inside

blocks.note: Donald TRUMP, the US president, without the last letter
ants are social insects, and a worker ant is the crossword's usual worker

explanation.surface: An Irishman's social worker gets an audience with the president, almost.
explanation.walkthrough: Paddy looks like an Irish name, but a paddy is British slang for a fit of temper. T(ANT)RUM; the 's stands for 'has'.
explanation.definitionFit: A paddy, in British informal speech, is an outburst of bad temper, the same thing as a tantrum.

clue.text: Devise it ultimately to stop celebrity getting upset by malicious critic

indicators.note: 'ultimately' means at the last, so only the last letter of 'it' is used
a stopper plugs a gap, so the single letter goes inside the turned word

blocks.note: to hatch a plan is to devise it
a big name is a celebrity
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A celebrity is upset by a nasty reviewer and plots to shut them up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting upset' looks like the celebrity's feelings, but in an across clue it turns the word round, and 'to stop' plugs a letter into it.
explanation.definitionFit: A hatchet man is someone employed to attack reputations or carry out ruthless tasks, figuratively wielding an axe.

clue.text: Wind the French right up with marches in Strasbourg initially

indicators.note: 'initially' takes only the opening letter of each of the last three words
in a down entry, 'up' means the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: first letters of three words
la is the feminine form of 'the' in French
RT is a standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: French right-wingers wind people up with protest marches in Strasbourg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind' reads as the verb wind up; it is the noun. The French wind makes the Strasbourg setting apt.
explanation.definitionFit: The mistral is a strong, cold northerly wind blowing down the Rhône valley into southern France.

clue.text: Rebel Frenchman for example brought back without notice

indicators.note: 'without' in its old sense of outside

blocks.note: René is a typical French man's name
e.g., exempli gratia
an ad, advertisement, is a notice

explanation.surface: A French rebel is sent home without any warning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without notice' is an idiom in the surface, but here 'without' is used in its old sense of outside, wrapping around the notice.
explanation.definitionFit: A renegade is someone who deserts a cause or rebels against authority, the noun sense of rebel.

clue.text: To criticise is mean

blocks.note: to find fault with or nag someone persistently
read as a verb: to intend or imply, as in asking what someone is driving at

explanation.surface: A moral judgement: finding fault with people is unkind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean' pretends to be the adjective unkind; it is the verb to intend or imply.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb has two senses: to nag or pick on someone, and to imply or intend.

clue.text: Determined after having gained from an unexpected outcome

blocks.note: to be up is to be ahead, having gained, as in being up on the deal
set on something means determined to do it

explanation.surface: Someone is determined to profit from a surprise result.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a gambler cashing in on a shock result, which is exactly what the answer names.
explanation.definitionFit: In sport an upset is a surprise victory by the outsider, a result nobody predicted.

clue.text: Often oddly neglected around fashionable Nice

indicators.note: the letters in odd positions are neglected, leaving only the even ones

blocks.note: letters two and four of the word
in means fashionable, as in 'the in thing'

explanation.surface: Fashionable Nice, the Riviera city, is often overlooked.
explanation.walkthrough: Nice looks like the French city because it opens the surface's last phrase with a capital; it is the adjective pleasant.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine and nice are both mild words of approval meaning pleasant or satisfactory.

clue.text: Term of imprisonment for unfortunate person overheard on street

indicators.note: something overheard is heard rather than read, so the sound counts

blocks.note: St is the standard abbreviation for street
a wretch is a miserable, unlucky person

explanation.surface: A homeless unfortunate is overheard on the street talking about prison.
explanation.walkthrough: The silent W in the person word drops out when spoken, leaving a word meaning to heave.
explanation.definitionFit: Stretch is British slang for a prison sentence, as in doing a five-year stretch.

clue.text: Provisional offering from Pinter impressed

indicators.note: the answer is offered up from within the run of the final two words

blocks.note: runs across the playwright's name and the next word

explanation.surface: A playwright's provisional new work impresses the critics.
explanation.walkthrough: Harold Pinter, the playwright, lends all but his first letter; the remaining three come from 'impressed'.
explanation.definitionFit: Interim means temporary, serving for a time until something permanent is arranged.

clue.text: Spelt out in some detail by Gable and Flynn perhaps

indicators.note: the phrase is spelt out afresh, its letters set down in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters

explanation.surface: A biography sets out the lives of two Hollywood stars in careful detail.
explanation.walkthrough: Clark Gable and Errol Flynn were handsome Hollywood leading men of the 1930s and 1940s; 'perhaps' marks them as examples.
explanation.definitionFit: A matinee idol is a handsome actor adored by audiences, a type both stars exemplified.
